strengths: The paper addresses an important question: how adversarial training can retain good clean generalization while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap.

Local robust memorization and the decomposition into signal learning and noise memorization provide an interpretable hypothesis. Combining representation complexity with training dynamics is a well-motivated approach.

The manuscript includes capacity sweeps on MNIST and CIFAR10, synthetic feature trajectories, and additional flatness diagnostics. The extensive appendices make the proposed arguments available for scrutiny.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution supported on two well-separated points, with a small clean classifier whose decision boundary lies near one point. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3. Once both points occur with nonvanishing training frequency, o(1) robust training error forces zero robust population error, making CGRO impossible. Additional assumptions controlling population coverage by training neighborhoods and the sample-size regime are essential.

The representation construction also has major proof gaps. Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes, but does not make same-class training balls disjoint, as asserted in Lemma 4.5; consequently, the subsequent algebraic rewriting need not hold. Appendix F then claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous function by continuous ReLU networks. Softening an indicator does not establish this approximation or preserve classification errors without additional margin and boundary-mass arguments.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robustness under the definitions in Section 3. Training perturbs only the signal direction and protects every noise patch, whereas robust training error concerns the full norm ball. Convergence of the restricted loss cannot imply small full-ball robust training error. Indeed, under the claimed feature scalings, an ℓ2 attack can reverse the noise patches and sufficiently attenuate the signal within the budget, producing negative training margins. The threat model must be made consistent throughout.

The clean-generalization proof in Appendix E.12 incorrectly treats a cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise as sub-Gaussian and uses a concentration expression that does not account for correlations across filters. Even a single nonzero cubed Gaussian is not sub-Gaussian. The inference from aggregate noise memorization to a constant norm for every orthogonal weight component is also unjustified. These steps are central to the claimed o(1) clean test error.

The synthetic experiment sets δ = α = 10, violating the theorem's strict δ < α condition and permitting complete signal removal. It therefore does not validate the stated theoretical regime. The empirical robustness evaluation also lacks attack step counts, step sizes, restarts, and variability across runs, limiting reproducibility and confidence in the reported robust accuracies.

The contribution relative to Li et al. (2022) needs sharper justification. Linearly separable hard instances already belong to the class admitting polynomial-size clean classifiers, so broadening that assumption alone does not strengthen an existential worst-case lower bound. The capacity experiments also do not establish that this worst-case expressivity barrier causes the observed training behavior. These positioning concerns are secondary to the correctness issues affecting both principal theoretical claims.
